_meta.title: Solving equations graphically or by systematic guess-check-refine
_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to solve equations graphically or by systematic guess-check-and-refine, using digital tools.

toLevel2.question: A graphical solution to an equation is found by identifying the y-coordinate of the point where two graphs intersect.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The x-coordinate of the intersection gives the solution, not the y-coordinate.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Confuses x and y coordinates at an intersection; the solution is the x-value, not the y-value.

toLevel2.question: The guess-check-refine method produces exact solutions to equations in every situation where it is applied.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Guess-check-refine produces successive approximations that converge toward the solution but typically yield only an approximate value.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Assumes iterative methods always terminate at the exact answer; in practice they approach but may not reach it.

toLevel2.question: Solving an equation graphically requires plotting both sides of the equation as separate functions and finding their intersection.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Setting f(x) = g(x) is equivalent to finding where y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect on the same set of axes.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May think only one graph is needed, or that rearranging to f(x) − g(x) = 0 is the only valid graphical approach.

toLevel2.question: Digital graphing tools can only find solutions to linear and quadratic equations and cannot handle higher-degree equations.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Digital tools graph any computable function, including cubics, transcendental, and other equations that resist algebraic solution.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Underestimates the capability of technology; modern tools handle arbitrary functions graphically and numerically.

toLevel2.question: In the guess-check-refine method, each successive guess should be informed by whether the previous result was too high or too low.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Using feedback from each iteration narrows the search interval systematically, driving convergence toward the solution.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May believe guesses are random; the method's power lies in using feedback to direct subsequent attempts.

toLevel2.question: An equation that has no algebraic solution also has no graphical solution and cannot be solved by any method.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Many equations without closed-form algebraic solutions can still be solved approximately using graphical or numerical methods.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Confuses algebraic insolubility with complete insolubility; graphical and numerical methods extend beyond algebra.

toLevel2.question: When solving an equation graphically, the number of intersection points between two curves indicates the number of solutions the equation has.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Each intersection represents a distinct x-value satisfying both equations, so the count of intersections equals the number of solutions.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May not connect geometric intersections with algebraic solutions; each crossing corresponds to exactly one solution.

toLevel2.question: A graphical solution provides the same level of precision as an exact algebraic solution in all circumstances.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Graphical solutions are limited by screen resolution and scale; they provide approximations unless the intersection falls on an exact pixel.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Assumes graphs give exact values; in practice, reading coordinates from a graph introduces rounding and visual error.

toLevel2.question: The systematic guess-check-refine method is also known as a numerical or iterative approach to solving equations.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Iterative numerical methods repeatedly refine estimates, which is precisely what guess-check-refine does in a structured manner.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May not recognise the formal name for this strategy; guess-check-refine is an introductory form of iterative numerical solving.

toLevel2.question: If two graphs do not intersect anywhere on the visible window, the equation necessarily has no solutions at all.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The graphs may intersect outside the visible window; absence of an intersection on screen does not prove no solution exists.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Assumes the visible portion shows the entire domain; graphs may intersect beyond the displayed range.

toLevel2.question: To solve the equation f of x equals zero graphically, one can plot y equals f of x and identify where the graph crosses the horizontal axis.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The x-intercepts of y = f(x) are the values where f(x) = 0, which are the solutions to the equation.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May confuse x-intercepts with y-intercepts; crossing the x-axis corresponds to f(x) = 0.

toLevel2.question: The guess-check-refine method requires the user to start with a guess that is already very close to the correct answer.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Any reasonable starting guess within the search interval will converge; the method systematically narrows down regardless of how close the initial guess is.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Assumes a good initial guess is mandatory; the bisection variant works from any interval that brackets the solution.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes what it means to solve an equation graphically?
toLevel2.correct: Finding the x-coordinates where two plotted functions intersect on the same axes
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Graphical solution locates the input values where both functions yield the same output, shown as intersection points.

distractors.answer: Drawing a single function and reading the y-intercept from the vertical axis
distractors.explanation: The y-intercept gives the value at x = 0, not the solution to a general equation.

distractors.answer: Calculating the gradient of a straight line drawn between two selected data points
distractors.explanation: Gradient calculation is unrelated to solving equations; it measures rate of change.

distractors.answer: Shading the region below a curve to determine the area enclosed by the function
distractors.explanation: Area under a curve relates to integration, not to solving equations for specific x-values.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly states the main advantage of graphical or numerical methods over algebraic methods for equation solving?
toLevel2.correct: They can find approximate solutions to equations that have no closed-form algebraic solution
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Many equations (e.g., transcendental) cannot be solved exactly; graphical and numerical methods provide practical approximations.

distractors.answer: They always produce exact rational answers with no rounding required at any stage
distractors.explanation: Graphical and numerical methods produce approximations, not exact values; rounding is inherent in these approaches.

distractors.answer: They eliminate the need for any understanding of the underlying mathematical functions involved
distractors.explanation: Understanding the functions helps set appropriate windows and starting values; the methods do not eliminate this need.

distractors.answer: They guarantee finding every solution within a single computation regardless of equation complexity
distractors.explanation: These methods may miss solutions outside the chosen window or interval; thoroughness requires careful setup.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly identifies the first step in solving an equation using the guess-check-refine method?
toLevel2.correct: Choose an initial estimate for the unknown value and substitute it into the equation to evaluate the result
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The process begins by testing a trial value, then comparing the outcome to the target to determine whether to adjust up or down.

distractors.answer: Rearrange the equation into standard quadratic form and apply the quadratic formula directly
distractors.explanation: The quadratic formula is an algebraic method; guess-check-refine does not require algebraic rearrangement.

distractors.answer: Plot both sides of the equation on a graphing calculator and zoom to the intersection point immediately to determine the answer
distractors.explanation: This describes graphical solution, not the guess-check-refine numerical method.

distractors.answer: Factor the equation completely and set each factor equal to zero to find all solutions
distractors.explanation: Factoring is an algebraic technique; guess-check-refine works iteratively without factoring.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following describes what a digital graphing tool displays when an equation has two solutions?
toLevel2.correct: Two distinct intersection points between the plotted curves on the coordinate plane
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Each solution corresponds to an intersection point; two solutions produce two visible crossings within the viewing window.

distractors.answer: A single intersection point that represents both solutions simultaneously as a combined value
distractors.explanation: Each solution is a separate x-value with its own intersection point; they cannot be combined into one.

distractors.answer: A highlighted vertical line segment connecting the two solution values on the y-axis
distractors.explanation: Solutions are x-values, not y-axis segments; they appear as distinct intersection points.

distractors.answer: An error message indicating that the equation is inconsistent and has no valid solutions
distractors.explanation: Multiple solutions do not produce errors; they simply appear as multiple intersection points on the graph.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly identifies a limitation of solving equations graphically using digital tools?
toLevel2.correct: The accuracy of the solution depends on the resolution and scale of the graphing window selected
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A coarse scale or small window may prevent precise reading of intersection coordinates, limiting accuracy.

distractors.answer: Graphical tools cannot display functions with negative y-values anywhere on the coordinate plane
distractors.explanation: All standard graphing tools display negative values; there is no such limitation.

distractors.answer: Digital tools require the equation to be polynomial before any graph can be generated or displayed
distractors.explanation: Digital tools graph transcendental, piecewise, and arbitrary functions, not only polynomials.

distractors.answer: The method fails entirely whenever the equation has more than one solution within the viewing window
distractors.explanation: Multiple solutions appear as multiple intersections; the method handles them naturally.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes the role of feedback in the guess-check-refine process?
toLevel2.correct: Determining whether the current estimate is too high or too low and adjusting the next guess accordingly
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing the evaluated result to the target reveals the direction of error, guiding the refinement of subsequent estimates.

distractors.answer: Confirming that the final answer is always exact and requires no further decimal place accuracy
distractors.explanation: The method produces approximations; feedback helps improve accuracy but does not guarantee an exact answer.

distractors.answer: Eliminating the need for any calculation by relying solely on visual inspection of the equation
distractors.explanation: Each iteration requires substitution and evaluation; feedback does not remove the need for calculation.

distractors.answer: Resetting the process to the original equation whenever the estimate exceeds a predetermined threshold
distractors.explanation: The method refines continuously toward the solution; there is no reset mechanism in standard practice.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly explains why the equation x cubed equals 3x plus 2 can be solved graphically?
toLevel2.correct: Plotting y equals x cubed and y equals 3x plus 2 and identifying where they cross each other
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The solutions satisfy both equations simultaneously, appearing as intersection points of the two graphs.

distractors.answer: Substituting x equals 1 into both sides to confirm equality and declaring that as the only solution
distractors.explanation: While x = 1 may be a solution, graphical methods reveal all solutions, not just one found by substitution.

distractors.answer: Factoring x cubed minus 3x minus 2 completely and reading the solutions from the factored form
distractors.explanation: This is an algebraic approach; graphical solution involves plotting, not factoring.

distractors.answer: Differentiating both sides and setting the derivatives equal to find the tangent intersection points
distractors.explanation: Setting derivatives equal finds where slopes match, not where the original functions intersect.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes an approximate solution from an exact solution to an equation?
toLevel2.correct: An approximate solution is a decimal near the true answer; an exact solution has no rounding
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Approximate solutions involve truncation or rounding; exact solutions are expressed in precise form (fractions, surds, symbols).

distractors.answer: An approximate solution uses fractions while an exact solution always uses recurring decimal representations
distractors.explanation: Fractions are exact forms; this reverses the relationship between fractions and approximations.

distractors.answer: An approximate solution can only be found algebraically while exact solutions require graphical methods to determine
distractors.explanation: The opposite is more common: algebra gives exact solutions and graphs give approximations.

distractors.answer: There is no meaningful distinction because all mathematical solutions are inherently approximate by nature
distractors.explanation: Mathematics distinguishes clearly between exact symbolic answers and rounded decimal approximations.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly identifies when the guess-check-refine method is particularly useful?
toLevel2.correct: When the equation cannot be solved by standard algebraic techniques such as factoring or applying a formula
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Guess-check-refine is most valuable precisely when algebraic methods fail or are impractical for the given equation type.

distractors.answer: When the equation is a simple linear equation that can be solved in a single algebraic step
distractors.explanation: Simple linear equations are solved instantly by algebra; numerical methods add unnecessary complexity.

distractors.answer: When the equation has already been solved and the answer needs to be verified by a different method
distractors.explanation: While verification is possible, the primary purpose is finding unknown solutions, not checking known ones.

distractors.answer: When exact symbolic answers are required and no decimal approximation will be accepted as valid
distractors.explanation: Guess-check-refine produces approximations; it is unsuitable when only exact answers are acceptable.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following describes what happens when a graphing tool zooms in on an intersection point?
toLevel2.correct: The coordinates of the intersection become more precisely identifiable as the scale decreases around the crossing
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Zooming reduces the scale, allowing finer reading of the x and y values at the intersection point.

distractors.answer: The intersection point disappears because the curves appear parallel at high magnification levels
distractors.explanation: Curves that cross still cross at any zoom level; they appear parallel only if they do not actually intersect.

distractors.answer: A new intersection point is created by the zooming process that did not exist at the original scale
distractors.explanation: Zooming does not alter the mathematics; the number of intersections is unchanged by scale adjustments.

distractors.answer: The tool automatically rounds the intersection coordinates to the nearest whole number for display
distractors.explanation: Zooming reveals more decimal places, not fewer; tools display coordinates at the precision of the current scale.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly states why solving equations graphically reflects professional mathematical practice?
toLevel2.correct: Scientists and engineers routinely use graphing software to solve complex equations that arise in modelling and analysis
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Professional practice involves digital tools for equations that exceed the scope of manual algebraic techniques.

distractors.answer: Professional mathematicians never use algebraic methods and rely exclusively on graphical tools for all equation solving
distractors.explanation: Algebra remains fundamental; graphical methods supplement rather than replace algebraic approaches.

distractors.answer: Graphical solutions are used only in educational settings and have no application in industry or research
distractors.explanation: Industry and research rely heavily on graphical and numerical methods for complex real-world equations.

distractors.answer: The primary purpose of graphing in professional practice is to create visually appealing presentations rather than to solve problems
distractors.explanation: While visualisation aids communication, the primary purpose of graphing tools in practice is problem solving.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly identifies the output of a single iteration in the guess-check-refine process?
toLevel2.correct: A refined estimate that is closer to the true solution than the previous guess based on the comparison result
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Each iteration uses the too-high or too-low feedback to produce a better approximation, narrowing the search interval.

distractors.answer: The exact algebraic solution expressed as a simplified fraction or radical that requires no further refinement
distractors.explanation: Single iterations produce approximations, not exact solutions; multiple iterations are needed to approach the answer.

distractors.answer: A proof that no solution exists for the equation within the domain of real numbers under consideration
distractors.explanation: Iterations approach solutions; failure to converge may indicate issues but a single step does not prove non-existence.

distractors.answer: A factored form of the original equation that reveals all solutions simultaneously without further computation
distractors.explanation: Guess-check-refine is numerical, not algebraic; it does not produce factored forms.

toLevel2.sentence: To solve f(x) = g(x) graphically, plot both functions and identify the {{blank:1}} of their intersection, which gives the {{blank:2}} of the equation.

blanks.correctExplanation: The x-value at the intersection satisfies both equations simultaneously and is the solution.

distractors.answer: y-coordinate
distractors.explanation: The y-coordinate gives the common output value, not the solution to the equation.

distractors.answer: gradient
distractors.explanation: The gradient at the intersection describes slope, not the solution value.

blanks.correctExplanation: The x-value where both graphs meet is the value that satisfies the original equation.

distractors.answer: gradient
distractors.explanation: The gradient is the rate of change, not the value that solves the equation.

distractors.answer: asymptote
distractors.explanation: An asymptote is a line the graph approaches; it is unrelated to intersection-based solutions.

toLevel2.sentence: In guess-check-refine, if substituting a trial value gives a result that is too {{blank:1}}, the next guess should be adjusted {{blank:2}}.

blanks.correctExplanation: If the evaluated result exceeds the target, the trial value overestimates the solution.

distractors.answer: precise
distractors.explanation: Precision refers to decimal places, not to whether the result overshoots or undershoots the target.

distractors.answer: complex
distractors.explanation: Complexity of the expression is irrelevant to the directional feedback used in refinement.

blanks.correctExplanation: When the result is too high, reducing the trial value moves the next estimate toward the actual solution.

distractors.answer: upward
distractors.explanation: Adjusting upward when already too high moves further from the solution, not closer.

distractors.answer: randomly
distractors.explanation: Random adjustment defeats the systematic nature of the method; directed adjustment ensures convergence.

toLevel3.question: When solving x cubed minus x equals 5 by guess-check-refine, testing x equals 2 gives 6 which is too high, so the next guess should be greater than 2.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Since 2 cubed minus 2 equals 6 which exceeds 5, the next guess should be less than 2 to reduce the output toward the target.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Reverses the direction of adjustment; a too-high result means the guess must decrease.

toLevel3.question: If a graphing tool shows that y equals x squared and y equals 2x plus 3 intersect at two points, then the equation x squared equals 2x plus 3 has exactly two real solutions.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Each intersection point corresponds to one real solution; two intersections mean exactly two real solutions exist.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May doubt the one-to-one correspondence between intersections and solutions; each crossing is one distinct solution.

toLevel3.question: When using guess-check-refine to solve an equation to two decimal places, the process always terminates after exactly two iterations.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The iteration count depends on starting proximity and equation behaviour; two decimal places may require many iterations to achieve.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Confuses decimal places of precision with number of iterations needed; these are independent quantities.

toLevel3.question: Rearranging f(x) = g(x) as f(x) minus g(x) equals zero and finding where the combined graph crosses the x-axis is not a valid graphical method.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Plotting h(x) = f(x) − g(x) and finding x-intercepts is algebraically equivalent to finding intersections of f and g; it is a valid alternative.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Does not recognise the algebraic equivalence between intersection of two curves and x-intercepts of their difference.

toLevel3.question: A graphical approach can reveal that an equation has no real solutions if the two plotted curves do not intersect anywhere across their entire domains.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: No intersection across the full domain means no x-value satisfies both equations simultaneously, confirming no real solution exists.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May confuse a limited viewing window with the full domain; if the entire domain is checked and no crossing exists, there is genuinely no solution.

toLevel3.question: The bisection method tests random points within the search interval rather than systematically choosing the midpoint at each step.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Bisection always tests the midpoint; systematic halving is its defining characteristic, not random sampling.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Confuses bisection with random search; bisection is deterministic, always selecting the interval midpoint.

toLevel3.question: When solving an equation graphically, the viewing window has no effect on the number of solutions visible on the display.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Solutions outside the viewing window are invisible; changing the window can reveal or hide intersection points.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Assumes all solutions are always visible; intersections beyond the displayed range require window expansion to see.

toLevel3.question: If guess-check-refine for the equation x cubed equals 10 gives x equals 2.15 as too low and x equals 2.16 as too high, the solution lies between these values.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A sign change (too low to too high) between consecutive test values guarantees the true solution lies within that interval.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: May not recognise the intermediate value theorem principle underlying the bracketing; a sign change confirms the solution is between the bounds.

toLevel3.question: A student uses a graphing tool to solve x cubed equals 3x plus 2 and sees three intersection points. Which one of the following correctly interprets this result?
toLevel3.correct: The equation has three real solutions, each corresponding to an x-coordinate where the cubic and linear graphs cross
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Three intersections mean three distinct x-values satisfy x³ = 3x + 2; each crossing is one solution.

distractors.answer: The equation has one solution that appears three times because the cubic is a third-degree polynomial function
distractors.explanation: Degree indicates the maximum number of solutions, not repetition; three crossings mean three distinct solutions.

distractors.answer: Only the middle intersection gives the correct solution and the outer two are graphical artefacts from the tool
distractors.explanation: All intersections of correctly plotted graphs represent valid solutions, not artefacts.

distractors.answer: The three intersections indicate that the equation is inconsistent and therefore has no valid real solutions
distractors.explanation: Intersections confirm solutions exist; inconsistency would mean no intersections at all.

toLevel3.question: When applying guess-check-refine to solve x cubed minus x equals 5, a student finds that x equals 1.9 gives 4.959 and x equals 2.0 gives 6.0. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
toLevel3.correct: Test x equals 1.95 because the solution lies between 1.9 and 2.0, and the midpoint narrows the interval efficiently
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Since 4.959 < 5 < 6.0, the solution is between 1.9 and 2.0; testing the midpoint bisects the interval.

distractors.answer: Conclude that x equals 1.9 is the answer because 4.959 is close enough to 5 for practical purposes
distractors.explanation: Without a specified tolerance, 4.959 may not meet precision requirements; further refinement is needed.

distractors.answer: Test x equals 3.0 because the result at x equals 2.0 was too large and a much smaller value is needed
distractors.explanation: Since the solution is between 1.9 and 2.0, jumping to 3.0 moves away from the answer, not toward it.

distractors.answer: Restart the process with x equals 0 because the current interval does not contain the solution
distractors.explanation: The sign change between 4.959 and 6.0 relative to 5 confirms the solution is in the interval; restarting wastes progress.

toLevel3.question: A student graphs y equals sin x and y equals x divided by 2 on the same axes. The curves intersect at the origin and at two other points. Which one of the following correctly explains why?
toLevel3.correct: Both functions equal zero at the origin, and the sine curve oscillates above and below the line, creating additional crossings
toLevel3.correctExplanation: sin(0) = 0/2 = 0 gives the origin; the sinusoidal oscillation guarantees further intersections where the wave crosses the line.

distractors.answer: The two additional intersections are errors caused by the graphing tool displaying sine values incorrectly near the extremes
distractors.explanation: Standard tools plot sine accurately; the additional intersections are genuine mathematical solutions.

distractors.answer: Only the origin is a true solution because sine and linear functions can intersect at most once by definition
distractors.explanation: No such limitation exists; a sinusoidal and linear function can intersect multiple times.

distractors.answer: The three intersections exist only because the viewing window is too wide and would disappear if the window were reduced
distractors.explanation: Reducing the window may hide intersections from view, but it does not eliminate them mathematically.

toLevel3.question: A student solves 2 to the power x equals 5 graphically and obtains x approximately equals 2.32. Which one of the following explains how to verify this answer?
toLevel3.correct: Substitute x equals 2.32 into 2 to the power x and confirm the result is close to 5
toLevel3.correctExplanation: 2^2.32 ≈ 4.99, which is close to 5, confirming the graphical solution is accurate to two decimal places.

distractors.answer: Check that 2 multiplied by 2.32 equals 5, verifying the linear relationship between base and exponent
distractors.explanation: 2 × 2.32 = 4.64 ≠ 5; this treats the exponential as linear multiplication, which is incorrect.

distractors.answer: Verify that log base 5 of 2 equals 2.32, since this is the inverse operation of exponentiation with base 5
distractors.explanation: The correct verification uses log base 2, not base 5; log₂(5) ≈ 2.32.

distractors.answer: Confirm that 5 squared equals 2.32, since squaring reverses the exponential operation applied to the base
distractors.explanation: 5² = 25 ≠ 2.32; squaring is unrelated to solving 2ˣ = 5.

toLevel3.question: When solving an equation graphically, a student notices the two curves appear to touch at one point without crossing. Which one of the following correctly describes this situation?
toLevel3.correct: The equation has a repeated solution at that point where the curves are tangent to each other
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Tangency means the curves meet but do not cross; algebraically this corresponds to a repeated root.

distractors.answer: The equation has no solutions because the curves must fully cross each other to produce a valid intersection
distractors.explanation: Tangent contact still satisfies both equations at that x-value; a full crossing is not required for a solution.

distractors.answer: The graphing tool has encountered a rounding error that creates a false appearance of contact between the curves
distractors.explanation: Tangent contact is a genuine mathematical phenomenon, not a computational error.

distractors.answer: The equation has infinitely many solutions in a neighbourhood around the point where the curves appear to meet
distractors.explanation: Tangency produces exactly one solution at the point of contact, not infinitely many.

toLevel3.question: A student uses guess-check-refine with interval halving to solve an equation. After 10 iterations starting from the interval from 0 to 1, which one of the following correctly estimates the precision achieved?
toLevel3.correct: Approximately three decimal places, because each halving reduces the interval width by a factor of 2
toLevel3.correctExplanation: After 10 halvings: 1/2¹⁰ = 1/1024 ≈ 0.001, giving precision to about 3 decimal places.

distractors.answer: Exactly ten decimal places, because each iteration reveals one additional decimal place of the answer
distractors.explanation: Each halving provides approximately 0.3 decimal places (log₁₀2 ≈ 0.3); 10 iterations give about 3, not 10.

distractors.answer: Only one decimal place, because bisection converges too slowly to achieve meaningful precision in ten steps
distractors.explanation: Ten halvings reduce the interval by a factor of 1024; this is sufficient for three decimal places.

distractors.answer: The precision cannot be estimated because bisection converges at an unpredictable rate depending on the equation
distractors.explanation: Bisection has a guaranteed, predictable convergence rate: one bit per iteration regardless of the equation.

toLevel3.question: Two students solve x squared plus 1 equals 0 using different methods. Student A uses algebra and finds no real solutions; Student B uses a graphing tool and sees no intersections. Which one of the following correctly compares their conclusions?
toLevel3.correct: Both methods correctly confirm no real solutions exist because x squared plus 1 is always positive and never equals zero
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The parabola y = x² + 1 lies entirely above the x-axis; graphically and algebraically, no real x satisfies the equation.

distractors.answer: Student B's graphical method is unreliable because it depends on the chosen viewing window and may miss solutions
distractors.explanation: For this equation, no window reveals an intersection because one genuinely does not exist for real x.

distractors.answer: Student A is incorrect because all quadratic equations have two real solutions by the fundamental theorem of algebra
distractors.explanation: The fundamental theorem guarantees complex roots; real solutions depend on the discriminant being non-negative.

distractors.answer: The methods contradict each other and a third method is needed to determine which student has the correct answer
distractors.explanation: Both methods agree on the same correct conclusion; there is no contradiction to resolve.

toLevel3.question: A student attempts to solve 2 to the power x equals negative 3 graphically. The graph of y equals 2 to the power x does not intersect y equals negative 3. Which one of the following correctly explains why?
toLevel3.correct: The exponential 2 to the power x is always positive for all real x and can never equal a negative value
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Since 2ˣ > 0 for all real x, the graph lies entirely above the x-axis and cannot reach y = −3.

distractors.answer: The graphing window is too small and expanding it sufficiently will reveal an intersection at a large negative x-value
distractors.explanation: No matter how far left the window extends, 2ˣ remains positive (approaching 0), never negative.

distractors.answer: The equation has a complex solution that the graphing tool cannot display on the standard real coordinate plane
distractors.explanation: While complex solutions may exist, the graphical method correctly shows no real solution; the explanation should address why.

distractors.answer: The student entered the equation incorrectly and the correct form would produce an intersection visible on the display
distractors.explanation: The equation is correctly stated; the absence of intersection reflects the mathematical impossibility, not input error.

toLevel3.question: A researcher models bacterial growth with an equation that has no algebraic solution. Which one of the following best justifies using a graphical method to find when the population reaches a target?
toLevel3.correct: Graphical methods provide usable approximate solutions for transcendental equations where algebraic manipulation cannot isolate the variable
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Transcendental equations resist algebraic isolation; graphing reveals intersection points that represent practical solutions.

distractors.answer: Graphical methods are chosen purely for visual appeal in presentations and offer no computational advantage over algebra
distractors.explanation: Graphical methods solve equations that algebra cannot; the choice is mathematical necessity, not aesthetics.

distractors.answer: Algebraic methods always work for growth models and the researcher should rearrange the equation more carefully instead
